prerequisites: Good knowledge of real and complex variable calculus
Good knowledge of functional analysis (representation and operations with real and complex variable functions)

learning_outcomes.text: Relate the theory of signals and systems within the algebraic theory of signal spaces and operator spaces.
Apply the general theory to both traditional system analysis and the mathematical modeling of physical problems.
Manage the general concept of transformation (transform) and frame the particular transformations addressed in the course within this concept.

Relate - establishing similarities and differences - discrete and continuous variable signal spaces with their associated usual algebra, as well as work with the signal parameters associated with each signal space.

Understand the particularization of general algebraic analysis to the case of continuous variable signals and systems, comprehending the need to introduce mathematical concepts associated with these spaces such as the theory of distributions or generalized functions.

Understand, apply, and operate the theory of continuous variable signals and systems: distribution theory, Fourier series expansion, Fourier transform, and Laplace transform viewed as particular cases of the general definition of transformation, as well as the spectral analysis of systems associated with these transformations, including simple examples of circuit analysis, modulations, filtering, etc.

Understand, apply, and operate the theory of discrete variable signals and systems: Fourier series expansion, Fourier transform, and Z transform viewed as particular cases of the general definition of transformation, as well as the spectral analysis of systems associated with these transformations, including simple examples of discrete systems.
Be able to operate in both continuous and discrete variables, understanding the relationship between both signal spaces.

Be able to apply the concepts of ideal signal sampling to relate both continuous and discrete variable signals and systems, as well as the transformed domains previously analyzed in continuous and discrete variables, and design simple continuous systems in terms of discrete systems.

syllabus_topics: Relationship between algebra/calculus and signal and system theory
Review of vector spaces and particularization of signal spaces
Introduction to the theory of distributions
Definition of the Dirac delta and physical meaning
Relationship of the Dirac delta with the step function
Operations with distributions (derivatives, convolutions, product and system resolution)
Relationship of DSF with linear and invariant systems
Relationship between TF and linear and invariant systems
Spectral energy and power density for deterministic signals
Periodic signals: Fourier series expansion (DSF) of discrete signals
Definition of the DSF for discrete variable signals
Convergence of the DSF for discrete variable signals
Properties of the DSF for discrete variable signals
Examples of the DSF for discrete variable signals
Relationship of DSF with linear and invariant systems
Aperiodic signals: Fourier transform (TF) of discrete signals
Definition of the TF for discrete variable signals
Convergence of the TF for discrete variable signals
Properties of the TF for discrete variable signals
Examples of the TF for discrete variable signals
Relationship of the TF with linear and invariant systems
Continuous and discrete variable signals and systems
Sampling and recovery of continuous variable signals
Modeling of a continuous LTI system using a discrete LTI system
assessment_rules: For the ordinary call, the theoretical block (BT) grade is the ordinary exam (EXO) grade. The classroom practice (BPA) grade is the minimum of 10 or (PAE + 0.3 * CPAE). The laboratory practice (BPL) grade is calculated as 0.35 * (0.8 * P1 + 0.2 * T1) + 0.65 * (0.8 * P2 + 0.2 * T2). The final grade is 0.7 * BT + 0.1 * BPA + 0.2 * BPL. For the extraordinary call, the final grade is 0.7 * EXE + 0.1 * EPA + 0.2 * EPL. None of the grades obtained during the current course will be saved for subsequent courses, and grades from preceding courses will not be considered.
